content.content:
## Natives

`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.

A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. At the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). Walk calls the same method by reflection (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"). The compile stops in these cases:

- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).

To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. Until the switch-over, a compiled test cannot reach the interpreter's library's bindings.

The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:

- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.

The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Examples are `makeNN32FromZZ32WithSpecialCompilerHackForNN32ResultType` for a result and `makeZZ32FromNN32WithSpecialCompilerHackForNN32ArgumentType` for a parameter. So a binding over `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char` that names any other helper is a type error for the checker. Walk loads it, because it carries these types in `int` and `long`.

The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.

## Traps of the compiled path

- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit.
- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. Two calls die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839).

## The checker's gaps

`revival-changes.md` gives the rules. This section gives where the checker applies them, and where it does not yet.

- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the code generator refuses such a declaration (ledger row 701). A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. The compiled path does not leave out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. A program that declares such a trait does not compile: the code generator refuses the trait's `where` clause (ledger row 701). Where a generic type that the clause lists, as `List[\E\]`, gives the body of a member of the trait, the code generator crashes before it refuses the clause: 'E is not in the kind env' (ledger row 812). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

## The `fortress` commands

`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

## Running

    cd ProjectFortress
    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.

- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead: it gives the cause.

## Before an edit

Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. Both date from September 2026, so a status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.
## Natives

The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:

- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use it. Most bindings name one.
- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives").

Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:

- `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `Char` in `int`; `ZZ64` and `NN64` in `long`; `RR64` in `double`; `RR32` in `float`; `Boolean` in `boolean`;
- `String`, `FlatString` and `JavaString` in `String`; `ZZ` in `BigInteger`; `()` in `void`.

Walk refuses a helper's binding at load in these cases. The message names the string, and contains the words below, which a `load_exception_contains` key can match:

- The class or the method does not exist: 'not found' or 'names no static method of'.
- The result type, or a parameter type other than `self`'s, is not in the list above: 'no Java type carries the declared'.
- No method of that name, or more than one, has exactly the Java types of the list: 'has no overload that fits the declaration's types', or 'overloads that fit'.

Walk does not check `self`. It passes `self` as the helper's first Java parameter, read as that parameter's Java type. So a binding in a method of a program's own type loads, and a `String` parameter receives the type's name (ledger row 847). Bind a helper in a method only if the helper's first Java parameter carries the type of `self`, as `int` for a method of `ZZ32`.

A native declared over `String`, glue class or helper alike, receives the wrong text for a `CatString`: the name of the type, not its characters (ledger row 846). `||` builds a `CatString` when the joined string is longer than `maxLeafSize`, 32 characters by default. If a string that reaches such a native can come from `||`, pass it as `s.asFlatString` at the call of the native.

An `import java` written in a `.fss` file is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it. The compiled path's generated `import java` (`compiler.md`, "Natives") is not this one.

A glue class raises a Fortress exception that a `catch` sees by throwing a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `Int.java` there makes one, and its callers throw it:

    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
    return new FortressError(f);

A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java`). The string names the compiler's prelude's class for the exception. Under walk, that class does not load, and `StaticNativeApp` raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place. So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as `DivisionByZero` and `IntegerOverflow`. `ZZ32`'s `DIV` by zero raises `DivisionByZero` in this way. A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other exception from a native ends the run, as a division by zero in a glue class does.

## Running a program

    bin/fortress P.fss

- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.

## The model program

MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.

- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters.
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:55
- P-58 **Every native binding is a `builtinPrimitive` call naming a static helper.** A native binding is a library body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, the library's own form, and it keeps that form. Why: the language has no foreign-function interface, only a planned one, so the library's own practice decides the binding's form. Its string is to name a static Java method in `nativeHelpers/`, the compiled path's helpers, such as `"com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intLT"`, in place of a glue class of walk, which the compiled path cannot use (F-32). Walk is to load the named helper through a loader beside its glue classes. At the parse, before the checker, the compiled path is to rewrite each such body into a synthetic `import java` of the helper and a call, and to refuse a string that names no helper. The bindings move onto helpers step by step, and from the step that moves a binding, the compiled checker checks it against the helper's Java signature, not all at once at the switch-over. The other form, `import java` declarations written in the library itself, is not taken. F-32 counts the bindings that still name a glue class.

## 1. What changed and why

`m CHOOSE n` is the binomial coefficient. On a fixed-size type, a result that does not fit throws `IntegerOverflow` (section 4; P-73 names `CHOOSE`). The compiled path's helpers, which walk now calls too, broke this rule in two ways (the CHOOSE probe, `plan-24/probes/choose.md`, sections 4.2 and 4.3).

**Past the safe-bound table, a raw Java exception.**
- Each helper first folds `k` to `min(k, n-k)`.
- For `n` above its Pascal table, it then indexes a safe-bound table: `maxIntChooseSafeN[k-2]`, 15 entries for `k` = 2 to 16, or `maxLongChooseSafeN[k-2]`, 32 entries for `k` = 2 to 33.
- Its guard against a large `k` tested `k > 33` (`ZZ32`) and `kk > 66` (`ZZ64`), which lie past the tables' ends.
- So a folded `k` from 17 to 33 on `ZZ32`, or from 34 to 66 on `ZZ64`, threw `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, which no `catch` sees.
- Every coefficient in that region overflows. The smallest is `34 CHOOSE 17` = 2,333,606,220 on `ZZ32`, and `68 CHOOSE 34` = 28,453,041,475,240,576,740 on `ZZ64`. At `n` = 67, a `k` of 34 folds to 33, which is inside the table.

**A scratch array shared by parallel calls.** Each helper's slow path, `intSlowCautiousChoose` or `longSlowCautiousChoose`, wrote, divided and multiplied one static array. Calls that run at once, as the iterations of a Fortress loop do, corrupted each other. The results were wrong values, a false `IntegerOverflow`, or a raw `UnknownError`.

The edit, in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/`:
- `simpleIntArith.java`: the probe's patch as written. The guard is `k - 2 >= maxIntChooseSafeN.length` (`:212`). `intSlowCautiousChoose` allocates `int[] tempIntChooseArray = new int[k]` per call (`:162-163`), and the static field is gone.
- `simpleLongArith.java`: the same two changes, in the patch's form. The guard is `kk - 2 >= maxLongChooseSafeN.length` (`:185`). `longSlowCautiousChoose` allocates `long[] tempLongChooseArray = new long[k]` per call (`:136-137`), and the static field is gone. The array has at most 33 entries, because that path answers -1 for `n > 66` with `2k > 66`. The `(int)kk` cast below the guard now meets only `kk` ≤ 33.
- `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:789`: trait `ZZ32`'s `opr CHOOSE(self,b:ZZ32):ZZ32` names `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intOverflowingChoose` instead of `Int$Choose`.
- `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:882`: trait `ZZ64`'s `CHOOSE` names `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleLongArith.longOverflowingChoose` instead of `Long$Choose`.

Both helpers keep the team's algorithm, both tables and every public signature. `library_tests/IntegerChoose1.fss:13` still imports `intSlowCautiousChoose`, and its run passes (section 2).

`NN32`'s compiled `CHOOSE` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:806`) calls `simpleUnsignedIntArith.unsignedIntOverflowingChoose`, which calls `longOverflowingChoose` (`simpleUnsignedIntArith.java:80-82`). So it gains both fixes. Its binding in the one library (`FortressBuiltin.fss:448`) stays on `NN32$Choose`, as the brief says.

## 2. The tests, failing and passing

The order of work:
1. I wrote the tests and committed them (`a0a3bf443`).
2. Every failing run below ended before the edit was first built. `ant compileAll` started at 13:03:59 UTC; the last failing run, the Java sweep, ended at 13:03:45.
3. Then the fix, the build and the library order.
4. Then the passing runs.

The harness runs at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

The tests, in `ProjectFortress/`:

The probe's three, from `choose.patch`:
- `tests/ChooseHelperWalk.fss`, and `compiler_tests/ChooseHelperCompiled.fss` with its `.test` (link, run, PASS). Each binds the `ZZ32` helper by its own declaration. Each checks 20 exact values and 12 overflows, and `n CHOOSE 2` for `n` from 46342 to 65536 in a parallel loop.
- The guard `tests/ChooseZZ32Walk.fss`: the same checks on the library's operator.

Their `ZZ64` counterparts, mine, in the same form:
- `tests/ChooseHelperZZ64Walk.fss`, and `compiler_tests/ChooseHelperZZ64Compiled.fss` with its `.test`. Each binds the `ZZ64` helper by its own declaration.

(* Under walk, the ZZ64 CHOOSE helper gives the exact binomial coefficient, raises IntegerOverflow exactly where it does not fit, and keeps its values when called in parallel. *)
component ChooseHelperZZ64Walk
export Executable

hChoose(n: ZZ64, k: ZZ64): ZZ64 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleLongArith.longOverflowingChoose")

overflows(n: ZZ64, k: ZZ64): Boolean =
  try
    ignore(hChoose(n, k))
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => true
  end

pair(n: ZZ64): ZZ64 = if n MOD 2 = 0 then (n DIV 2) (n - 1) else n ((n - 1) DIV 2) end

chk(got: ZZ64, want: ZZ64, what: String): () = assert(got, want, what)

run():() = do
  maxL: ZZ64 = 9223372036854775807
  minL: ZZ64 = -maxL - 1
  (* basic-integers.tex, section "Integers", opr CHOOSE; opr-overview.tex, subsections "GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators" and "Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators" *)

  chk(hChoose(3037000501, 2), 4611686020018625250, "3037000501 CHOOSE 2")
  chk(hChoose(4294967296, 2), 9223372034707292160, "4294967296 CHOOSE 2")
  chk(hChoose(maxL, 1), maxL, "MAX CHOOSE 1")
  chk(hChoose(maxL, maxL - 1), maxL, "MAX CHOOSE (MAX - 1)")
  chk(hChoose(maxL, maxL), 1, "MAX CHOOSE MAX")
  chk(hChoose(3, 5), 0, "3 CHOOSE 5")
  chk(hChoose(5, -1), 0, "5 CHOOSE -1")

  assert(overflows(67, 33), "67 CHOOSE 33 throws IntegerOverflow")

end

hChoose(n: ZZ64, k: ZZ64): ZZ64 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleLongArith.longOverflowingChoose")

overflows(n: ZZ64, k: ZZ64): Boolean =
  try
    ignore(hChoose(n, k))
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => true
  end

nChoose(n: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): NN32 = unsigned(n) CHOOSE unsigned(k)

overflowsN(n: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): Boolean =
  try
    ignore(nChoose(n, k))
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => true
  end

pair(n: ZZ64): ZZ64 = if n MOD 2 = 0 then (n DIV 2) (n - 1) else n ((n - 1) DIV 2) end

chk(got: ZZ64, want: ZZ64, what: String): () = assert(got = want, what)

472 1022
component ChooseSkB
export Executable

(* oracle: n CHOOSE k by ZZ64 products with a gcd, -1 where it exceeds ZZ64 *)
exact(n: ZZ64, k: ZZ64): ZZ64 = do
  top: ZZ64 = 9223372036854775807
  var r: ZZ64 = 0
  if k >= 0 AND k <= n then
    kk: ZZ64 = if k > n - k then n - k else k end
    var acc: ZZ64 = 1
    var j: ZZ64 = 1
    var over: Boolean = false
    while j <= kk AND NOT over do
      m: ZZ64 = n - kk + j
      g: ZZ64 = acc GCD j
      a: ZZ64 = acc DIV g
      b: ZZ64 = m DIV (j DIV g)
      if a > top DIV b then over := true else acc := (a) (b) end
      j := j + 1
    end
    if over then r := -1 else r := acc end
  end
  r
end

want32(n: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): ZZ64 = do
  e: ZZ64 = exact(widen(n), widen(k))
  var r: ZZ64 = e
  if e > 2147483647 then r := -1 end
  r
end

ovf32(n: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): Boolean =
  try
    ignore(n CHOOSE k)
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => true
  end

ovf64(n: ZZ64, k: ZZ64): Boolean =
  try
    ignore(n CHOOSE k)
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => true
  end

got32(n: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): ZZ64 = do
  var r: ZZ64 = -1
  if NOT ovf32(n, k) then r := widen(n CHOOSE k) end

The \OPR{CHOOSE} operator is defined only for natural number types;
it computes the binomial coefficient \EXP{m \OPR{CHOOSE} n = m!/(n! (m-n)!)}.
If \EXP{n<0} or \EXP{n>m}, the result is \EXP{0}.

---

The handling of overflow depends on the type of the number produced.
For integer results, overflow throws an \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
Rational computations do not overflow.
The infix operator \OPR{GCD} computes the greatest common
divisor of its integer operands, and \OPR{LCM} computes the least
common multiple.  The operator \OPR{CHOOSE} computes binomial
coefficients:
\EXP{n \OPR{CHOOSE} k = \binom{n}{k} = { n! \over k!(n-k)! }}.

### The rule the rungs keep, and how they meet

- No two rungs change one declaration, and no rung builds on another rung (PLAN, "The principle for the batches"): each rung's tests pass on its own tree. None lands only with another.
- The declarations each rung changes. F: StaticNativeApp.javaFor, Float's 30 strings. Z: ZZ64's 20 strings and ZZ's 16. S: the 8 strings of Long, NN32, BigNum, Char, NN64 and char. K: the two CHOOSE helpers, their slow paths' scratch arrays, and the two CHOOSE strings. W: StaticNativeApp.find and the new javaForSelf, NativeApp.checkAndLoadNative, the constructors of FunctionClosure, MethodClosure and FunctionalMethod. G: CodeGen's three guards. H: BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter, the strings of NN32's 20, NN64's 17 and Char's 39. The Appendix I entry's Effect: the gather.
- Files two rungs share: StaticNativeApp.java (F, W); ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss (F, S, H); Library/FortressLibrary.fss (Z, S, K, H). The manifest's order is F, Z, S, K, W, G, H; by the gather's rule on shared files it applies F, K, Z, S, W, G, H (fork 1).
- They meet on the merged tree: W's check of self meets every moved binding, which the planner measured with F, Z and S (walk's suite 694, the one failure W's own XXX); the stages read all moved bindings, which the planner measured at 0 and 0 with all 83 moved; the family guards and climb batch 23's run together in walk's suite and the compiler track. H's 76 meet W's check of self too, over NN32, NN64 and Char, which the planner measured with W's prototype: the library's 97 helper bindings loading, H's values the old code's.

### The gate, and what it should show

The comparands are climb batch 23's `summary.txt`, `checker-count.txt` (0) and `distance.txt` (0, over the fourteen, setting compile), in `compile-ladder/climb-batch-23/gate/`.
- `testSystem`: 694, the comparand's sum (181, 169, 174 and 170), plus the planner's named walk tests: F 1, Z 4 (row 848's XXX test moved to H), S 3, K 4 (the probe's two and their ZZ64 counterparts), W 1 (the trait case; the promotion renames) and H 6 (three guards, two division tests, one XXX test), so about 713, and any more that the rungs add (climb batch 23's forecast counted only the planner's, and its gate had 4 more).
- `testFast`: the compiler track 1,338 plus F's, Z's and S's compiled guards (a link and a run each, 6) and G's (the promotion's link and run, 2; two run tests, 4; the run pair, 1 more), and K's (the probe's compiled test and its ZZ64 counterpart, a link and a run each, 4; the promotion turns an expected failure into a pass), and H's (three compiled guards and the rewrite's test, a link and a run each, 8; the XXX pair for row 860, 2), so about 1,365, and any more that the rungs add; the library track 86, the other-compiler track 263 and the misc track 440, as landed.
- `testSpecData`: 130 green.
- The four-thread atomic runs, 42 lines: unchanged; no rung touches the run time's tasks or transactions.
- The ladder: 85 programs at `pass`; no rung declares a move.
- The checker count: 0, reported, not declared, its 14 api rows as the comparand's; on the merged tree it reads Z's 36, S's 2, K's 2 and H's 17 in the main component.
- The distance, reported and never red (P-39): 0 over the fourteen, `#crash none`; on the merged tree it reads all 152, the batch's 76 that fit and H's 76; `compare.sh` prints 'DISTANCE SAME   0' and no setting line.
- The 52 team demos at the gather, each reaching its end (F-283).
- microGPT's quick pair at the commit stage, both programs `ALL PASS`, 7 of 7 each (P-30): the first landing at which walk's float arithmetic runs through helpers.

### The ledger

New rows go into `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md` only through `ledger.py add`, by the gather; until then a worker or a skeptic writes each new row in its `record.md` in the row template with the placeholder `NEW-<rung>-<n>`. Rows filed by plan before the launch: 855 (the CHOOSE helpers' race, the probe's draft), 856 (`signed` above the signed range), 857 (`char` out of range), 860 (the `NN64` wrapping negation's helper) and 861 (`Char`'s `asExprString` in two forms). Rows closed: 847 (W), 521 and 855 (K). Rewritten: 336 (Z), 848 (H), 701 (G). Reproducers set: 336 (Z), 848 and 860 (H), 856 and 857 (S). Notes: 307 (G). Where `ledger.py` refuses a note for length, the gather writes it by a rewrite, as climb batch 23's did for row 521.

### After the landing

The landing report; the routing of every item for the curator into PLAN, Question 1 and this record's forks and points among them (the post-batch review's finding 1); FACTS: F-32 (the 449, 173 moved), F-298 (the rewrite's transfers for `NN32`, `NN64` and `Char`), F-299 (its count, its CHOOSE and its row-847 sentences), F-181 (the `where` half), F-53 unchanged, and the CHOOSE probe's and the hard-set probe's facts (`choose.md` and `hard-set.md`, section 9 of each); the hard-set probe's Q2 and Q3 as review-queue items, and Question 2 on his review list; the skill writer's task with the batch's sentences made false; the post-batch review. The next natives batch takes `NN32`'s `CHOOSE`, H's four left on their glue classes as their rows are fixed, and the string family by item 310; the rest of the 109 waits for the answers to Q2 and Q3.

### Forks the batch takes, none consequential

Each default can be undone, and none reverses a decision of his or touches a line of microGPT.

1. **Seven rungs, F, Z, S, K, W, G and H, the manifest's order; none lands only with another; the gather applies them by its rule, F, K, Z, S, W, G, H.** Default: so. No rung builds on another: each one's tests pass on its own tree. F, Z and S share two library files, at different declarations; F and W share `StaticNativeApp.java`, at different declarations (fork 4); K shares `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` with Z and S, at the two `CHOOSE` declarations. The gather's rule puts two rungs that share a file in the ascending order of their lowest edited line in it, and keeps the manifest's order for rungs that share none (`climb-batch-workflow.md`, "Gather"): K's first string, `FortressLibrary.fss:789`, is above Z's, `:832`, and S's, `:986`, so K goes before Z and S; F goes before S (`FortressBuiltin.fss:56` against `:380`) and before W (`StaticNativeApp.java:51` against `:81`). No line moves by the order: every family hunk replaces one line with one; H's hunks at `FortressBuiltin.fss:610` and `FortressLibrary.fss:964` carry S's two changed lines as context, so after S they go in through the gather's `--3way`, which merges them clean (the review). W is applied after the families since its check of `self` meets every moved binding on the merged tree. H shares `FortressBuiltin.fss` with F and S and `FortressLibrary.fss` with Z, S and K, at different declarations, and shares no file with W or G: its lowest lines, `FortressLibrary.fss:918` and `FortressBuiltin.fss:392`, come after K's, Z's and F's; with S the two files order the pair both ways (S's `:380` before H's `:392`, H's `:918` before S's `:986`), so the pair keeps the manifest's order, S before H; and H keeps its manifest place after W and G, which share no file with it.
2. **K takes `CHOOSE` on both `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, as a rung of its own.** Default: the CHOOSE probe recommends `CHOOSE` in this batch with the helper's fix in the rung that moves the binding, the record deciding the fix (`plan-24/probes/choose.md`, sections 1 and 8: the specification's coefficient and its `IntegerOverflow`, P-73, row 521's fix); its patch fixes `simpleIntArith` only. K takes that patch and makes the same two fixes in `simpleLongArith`, whose same two faults the probe measured, and moves both `CHOOSE` bindings. The ways not taken: `ZZ32`'s alone, which leaves `XXXChooseTableCompiledRungE` an expected failure, since it asserts both helpers, and leaves `ZZ64`'s `CHOOSE` and row 855's `ZZ64` half to a later batch with no rung named; or the `ZZ64` half inside Z, which would put an edit of helpers that both paths run, and both paths' suites, into a rung of library text. A rung of its own: K edits two helpers that both paths run, so it runs both paths' suites, and Z stays library text with its tests.
3. **F carries walk's carry of `Float`, one line of `StaticNativeApp.javaFor`.** Default: so. Walk's loader carries a declared parameter type only by name, and `Float` is not among its names (`interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java:47-58`), so the planner's sample move of `Float`'s `+` alone stopped every program at load: 'Native helper com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleDoubleArith.doubleAdd: no Java type carries the declared type of parameter b.' Twelve of the 30 have a parameter declared `Float`. The ways not taken: the declarations rewritten at `RR64`, which changes `Float`'s headers and its overloads; the carry put in W, on which F's tests would then build.
4. **W's check of `self`: the closure tells the loader the type that declares the method, and the loader takes that type's Java carrier from its own table.** Default: `MethodClosure` passes its `definer` and `FunctionalMethod` its self type through `NativeApp.checkAndLoadNative` to `StaticNativeApp.find`, which refuses at load a method whose declaring type no Java type carries, 'Native helper ...: no Java type carries Holder, the type of self.', and takes only an overload whose first Java parameter is that carrier; a top-level function is told no type and is loaded as today. The table, `javaForSelf`, is `javaFor`'s names plus the value objects `Int`, `Long`, `UnsignedLong`, `Float` and `BigNum`, so W carries `Float` for `self` without F's line, and the two rungs change different declarations. The ways not taken: a refusal at the call, where row 847 asks for one at load; the declaring type read from the syntax tree, which has no parent links; one table shared with F's parameter carry, which two rungs would then both change.
5. **Two guards per family rung, the walk guard and the compiled guard.** Default: the walk guard in `ProjectFortress/tests/`, `NativeHelperFamily<Name>Walk.fss`, calls every binding the rung moves on chosen values, edge cases among them, asserts each result with the harness's own checks, and passes on the base's code and after; the compiled guard in `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/`, `NativeHelperFamily<Name>Compiled.fss` with its `.test` (link and run), binds the same helpers through its own top-level declarations, one per helper, the helper's Java signature read as the compile reads it (`self` as the first parameter, `JavaString` for `String`, `Character` for `Char`), asserts the same values, and passes on the base and after, since climb batch 23's rewrite already compiles such a declaration (F-298; the planner's sample, section 4). The compiled guard cannot declare a method on the prelude's number types, so it binds functions; it tests the code generator's call of each helper, which no compiled program can reach through the library until the switch-over. Neither guard asserts a value that a ledger row names as a departure or that the specification leaves open: a float compared with a NaN (row 672), the rounding of a NaN or an infinity (row 330), `signed` above the signed range and `char` outside the code points (section 4).
6. **Z's divisions by zero, as climb batch 23's `ZZ32` one.** Default: two tests, `ZZ64DivisionByZeroWalk` and `ZZDivisionByZeroWalk`, each a `DIV` by zero in a `try` that catches `DivisionByZero`, failing on the base ('java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero' and 'BigInteger divide by zero' in the planner's runs) and passing after; row 336 rewritten to what stays, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`; and the `XXX` test that the post-batch review's finding 7 owes the batch that edits row 336 (PLAN, "Climb batch 23, listed for his review"): `XXXZZ64RemainderByZeroWalk`, `widen(8) REM widen(0)` in a `try` that catches `DivisionByZero`, seen red through the harness on the base and set as row 336's reproducer. Row 848's half is H's, since H moves `NN32`'s and `NN64`'s `DIV` onto helpers that raise: H writes `NN32DivisionByZeroWalk` and `NN64DivisionByZeroWalk`, failing on the base and passing after, and row 848's owed `XXX` test over a remainder, `XXXNN32RemainderByZeroWalk`, `unsigned(7) REM unsigned(0)`; an `XXX` test over `NN32`'s `DIV`, as this record first gave Z, would turn red on the merged tree.
7. **The Appendix I entry's Effect is the gather's.** Default: no rung edits `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`. Its entry "A native binding that names a static helper" states the count of moved bindings, `CHOOSE`'s state, the divisions by zero that end the run, and row 847 (`changes.tex:4466-4502`), so F, Z, S, K, W and H each make a sentence of it false; one declaration changed by six rungs breaks the batch's rule. Each rung lists its sentences made false; the gather rewrites the Effect once on the merged tree, builds the specification once, and the commit stage takes that build if no later commit changes `Specification/` (the post-batch review's finding 4). `builtinPrimitive`'s printed comment (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:14-29`) holds no count and stays true; W makes its "%self% first" true for `self` too.
8. **The 52 team demos run by the gather** on the merged tree (F-283; P-79), as climb batch 23's fork 19. No rung runs them.
9. **The suites each rung runs, once, after its last change of code.** Default: F and W, which edit walk's Java, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData`; K, which edits helpers that a library string names and both paths run, and H, which edits the rewrite that the parser runs on the compiled path's repository, `ant testQuick` and `ant testSystem`; Z and S, which edit library text only, their own tests through the harness; G, which edits the code generator, its own tests, the tracks left to the gate (the `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite").
10. **The stages.** Default: F, Z, S, K and H run the count stage and the distance stage once each on their final trees, the check of their moved bindings (P-58; P-39); W and G run neither, since neither changes what the checker reads; the gather runs neither, since no row of this batch closes on a stage (the post-batch review's finding 4); the gate runs both.
11. **`truncate` and `round` move now, at `ZZ64`.** Default: so. Both fit today (`doubleTruncate` and `doubleRound` answer a Java `long`); P-68's rung after the switch-over gives them `ZZ` and meets their helpers then.
12. **G takes row 701's `where` half only.** Default: G drops the header `where`-clause condition at the three guards (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:2967`, `:4107`, `:5027`), and keeps the contract condition beside it; row 701 is rewritten to its contract half; row 812, a crash before the guard, stays (it holds nothing of this rung's tests). The exit judgement's default places the rung before the names batch, the coordinator's call (`reviews/phase3-exit/judgement.md`, item 9: "Not consequential (an ordering within decided ground); the coordinator takes it."); P-151 decides which forms exist, and a condition on static parameters, checked by the checker, emits no code.
13. **G's tests.** Default: `XXXWhereBoundChecker` promoted (a function with a `where` bound, which ran and printed 'O' in the planner's probe); two new run tests in `compiler_tests/`, a method whose `where` clause bounds its object's static parameter (`SumReduction`'s `distribute` and `BoundedRange.atMost` have that form) and a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause variable (`AnyList`'s form); and `XXXNatOpenRun`, whose compile no longer fails, turned into a run pair, `NatOpenRunLink.test` and `XXXNatOpenRun.test` with `REACHED`, for row 307's wall behind it: the call that reads a size off its argument ended in a `VerifyError` in the probe. Row 307 gains a note.
14. **No speed pass.** No rung changes the checker's code: G changes the code generator, which the stages do not run.
15. **No rung declares a checker count, a crash or a ladder move.** All 85 ladder programs pass at climb batch 23's gate, so none can move.
16. **Rows.** Default: W closes 847; K closes 521 and 855; Z rewrites 336 and sets its reproducer; S sets the reproducers of 856 and 857; H rewrites 848 and sets its reproducer and 860's; G rewrites 701 and notes 307. Rows filed by plan, before the launch, at the coordinator's word: 855, the race of the two `CHOOSE` helpers (the CHOOSE probe's draft), 856 (`signed` above the signed range), 857 (`char` out of range), 860 (the `NN64` wrapping negation's helper answers its operand) and 861 (`Char`'s `asExprString` in two forms). Any other defect a rung meets gets its row through its `record.md`, as the manual gives it.
17. **`FlatString`'s 5 left out.** Default: so, by his scope, which does not list them; they are declared over `FlatString`, so row 846 does not reach them, and the string family's batch can take them with or before item 310 (section 4).
18. **H moves 76 of the 82.** Default: of the 80 that the hard-set probe names (the 82 less `NN32`'s `asFloat`, fork 12, and `NN32`'s `CHOOSE`), H leaves four on their glue classes, since their helpers change a value under walk, measured: `UnsignedLong`'s `asString` and `asExprString`, whose helper prints an `NN64` above its signed half as negative (row 326); `NN64`'s prefix `DOTMINUS`, whose helper answers its operand (row 860); and `Char`'s `asExprString`, whose helper writes a character outside ASCII in another form (row 861). With the 80 moved for one run, 91 of 1,325 printed values changed, every one from those four; with them back, none. The ways not taken: H fixes the two `NN64` helpers (`Long.toUnsignedString`, `-a`), which would change the prelude's compiled `NN64` printing and `BOXMINUS` too and bring nativeHelpers into a rung of the rewrite; or moves them with the change of value, against the guard. `NN32`'s `CHOOSE` needs both K's helper fix and H's rewrite, so neither rung alone can test it: it waits for the next natives batch, one string, once both have landed.

### Points the batch lists for him, not questions

- **Team lines changed:** H, 76 strings of `value object NN32`, `trait NN64` and `value object Char`, and the revival's `BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter`; F, 30 strings of `value object Float` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:54-194`); Z, 36 strings of `trait ZZ64` and `trait ZZ` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:818-909`, `:991-1085`); S, 8 strings in both files; K, the two `CHOOSE` strings and one line in each of `simpleIntArith.intOverflowingChoose` and `simpleLongArith.longOverflowingChoose`; W, the team's `FunctionClosure`, `MethodClosure`, `FunctionalMethod` and `NativeApp.checkAndLoadNative`; G, three lines of the team's `CodeGen`. `StaticNativeApp` is the revival's.
- **What walk does differently:** `ZZ64`'s and `ZZ`'s `DIV` by zero raise `DivisionByZero`, where the run ended (row 336); a helper bound in a method of a type that no Java type carries is refused at load (row 847); `NN32`'s and `NN64`'s `DIV` by zero raise `DivisionByZero` (H; row 848). `CHOOSE` keeps its values: the fixed helper agrees with walk's glue class on every pair the probe swept (`choose.md`, section 7.1). No other value moves, by the planner's runs.
- **What the compiled path does differently:** a binding over `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char` is checked against its helper through the team's transfers, where the checker refused it (H); a header `where` clause compiles (G); the compiled `CHOOSE` past its table raises `IntegerOverflow` (row 521), and parallel calls of it no longer corrupt each other (row 855), on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and, through the `ZZ64` helper, `NN32`.
- **Walk's float arithmetic runs through reflection after F,** where its glue classes were compiled calls: the operations of microGPT's two programs. Walk's speed is no measure (P-29); the commit stage's quick microGPT check is where it shows, against P-30's minute. The planner did not time it, by the ruling of 2026-10-23 (PLAN, "Where we stand").

prog='''component ChooseSkE
export Executable

%s
ovfN(n: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): Boolean =
  try
    ignore(unsigned(n) CHOOSE unsigned(k))
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => true
  end

chkN(n: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): () = do
  e: ZZ64 = exact(widen(n), widen(k))
  var w: String = "OVF"
  if e =/= -1 AND e <= 4294967295 then w := "" || e end

run(): () = do
  for n <- 0:140 do
    for k <- 0:n do
      kk: ZZ32 = if k > n - k then n - k else k end
      if NOT (n > 66 AND kk >= 34) then chkN(n, k) end
    end
  end
  for n <- 46342:52000 do chkN(n, 2) end
  for n <- 92679:92685 do chkN(n, 2) end
  for n <- 1627:2960 do chkN(n, 3) end
  for n <- 339:600 do chkN(n, 4) end
  println("DONE")
end

end

content.content:
Until the compiled code moves onto \library, the type checker checks the moved
bindings, but no compiled program runs them.
Under the interpreter a helper's raise of \TYP{IntegerOverflow} or
\TYP{DivisionByZero} is the library's own exception, so \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}'s
\EXP{\div} by zero throws a \TYP{DivisionByZero}, as \chapref{operators} says of
an integer result; \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}'s \OPR{REM} and \OPR{MOD}, the three on
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and \EXP{\div} on \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, which still name glue
classes, end the run with a Java exception at a divisor of zero (row~336 of
the revival's gap ledger), and so do \EXP{\div}, \OPR{REM} and \OPR{MOD} on
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} and \OPR{REM} and \OPR{MOD} on
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (row~848 of the revival's gap ledger).
The interpreter passes a helper declared over \TYP{String}, as its glue classes
do, the name of the value's type in place of its characters where the value is
not a flat string, as a \TYP{String} made by concatenating two long strings
(row~846 of the revival's gap ledger).
The interpreter reads the \KWD{self} of a method only by the helper's Java
type, since it is not told the type that declares the method: a helper bound
in a method of a type that no Java type carries, as a program's own object,
is not refused, and its call passes the object as that Java type reads it,
the name of its type to a helper over \TYP{String} (row~847 of the
revival's gap ledger).
The compiler leaves a declaration with a varargs parameter as a call of
\VAR{builtinPrimitive}, so the type checker does not check such a binding
against its helper (row~849 of the revival's gap ledger); no binding of
\library\ that names a helper has a varargs parameter.
